proposal: The Mandate recommends moving the Office for Civil Rights to the Department of Justice, with the federal government enforcing civil rights through DOJ and the courts and OCR at DOJ enforcing only through litigation. status_summary: As of 2026-10-08 OCR remains part of ED, and the June 2026 arrangement with DOJ is announced but not shown to be operating at scale. ED's release (last-reviewed date 2026-06-16) announced agreements with the Department of Justice on civil rights enforcement, student privacy protection, and training and advisory services drawn from DOJ's school desegregation role; for civil rights enforcement it says the two agencies will combine capacities to evaluate, investigate and resolve civil rights complaints, that ED keeps all its statutory authorities and functions, and that enforcement continues without interruption. K-12 Dive and Littler, reading the agreement, report that OCR will refer complaints to DOJ's Civil Rights Division to evaluate, investigate and resolve, and may resolve complaints based on DOJ's proposed findings; Littler gives only the 2026-06-16 announcement date. Education Week (2026-07-27) reports that OCR will reimburse DOJ for these services, that the agreement does not say whether staff will transfer, and that no referrals or counts had been reported. K-12 Dive reports ED keeps leadership of OCR, the choice between administrative enforcement and DOJ referral, mediation, settlements, guidance and the Civil Rights Data Collection; officials said staffing and workload division would be worked out over the coming weeks. A 2026-09-15 Government Executive report does not list OCR among offices being reassigned and says laid-off OCR staff were asked to return and attorneys are being hired. This differs from the Mandate's design of moving OCR itself to DOJ and limiting enforcement to litigation.

timeline.event: During the fall 2025 shutdown ED issues layoff notices to about 500 more employees, including in OCR; the notices were later rescinded (month only; day not given).
ED's November 2025 agreements leave civil rights enforcement at ED while it explores options.

ED announces agreements with DOJ on civil rights enforcement, student privacy protection, and training and advisory services (alongside an HHS agreement on special education). For civil rights enforcement, ED's release says the agencies will combine capacities to evaluate, investigate and resolve complaints, that ED keeps all its statutory authorities and functions, and that enforcement continues without interruption; the release gives no staffing statements and the agreement text was not retrieved. K-12 Dive reports OCR will refer complaints to DOJ to evaluate, investigate and resolve, and that ED keeps oversight, leads OCR and decides between administrative enforcement and DOJ referral; officials describe it as a first step with staffing to be worked out over the coming weeks.
In Senate HELP markup, a Democratic amendment to bar the civil rights office move to DOJ fails on a party-line vote; S. 5046, which names four other ED offices, advances 13-9 without covering OCR.

title: Move the Office for Civil Rights to DOJ with litigation-only enforcement
uncertainties: The agreement text and the joint ED and DOJ fact sheet were not retrieved (the ed.gov agreement PDF returned HTTP 403 to an earlier researcher, and a civil rights partnership fact sheet on ed.gov located by search returned a fetch error to two researchers and in this review; ED's release mentions the fact sheet but its page text carries no link). ED's release was read through a fetch summary and has no printed release date; its last-reviewed date of 2026-06-16 matches the Education Week and K-12 Dive announcement date. The specific mechanics (referral of complaints, ED's retained choice of enforcement path, reimbursement) rest on K-12 Dive, Littler and Education Week, which read the agreement; ED's own release says only that the agencies combine capacities and that ED keeps its statutory authorities. No ED or DOJ release dated after 2026-06-16 on implementation was found, and no report of referrals in practice was found as of the Education Week piece of 2026-07-27. A signing date of June 15 appears only in a letter hosted by the National Women's Law Center, an advocacy group, and is an unverified lead at low confidence; Littler gives only the 2026-06-16 announcement date, which matches the last-reviewed date on ED's release. The same 2026-09-30 letter from 139 organizations is the only source for statements that the FY2026 appropriations law (Pub. L. 119-75) limits ED fund transfers and that the administration intends to delegate OCR enforcement to DOJ; these are unverified leads at low confidence, and the portions of the law text on govinfo.gov and of a CRS report on its Labor-HHS-Education division that were opened did not reach the Education provisions, so the transfer-limit claim was neither confirmed nor refuted. Which complaint types go to DOJ was not specified. Whether any OCR staff have been detailed to DOJ was not found. The 2025 OCR regional office closures and court cases over OCR layoffs were not researched by name. The Mandate's related recommendation to put OCR's Case Processing Manual through notice and comment (p. 357) was not checked. Month-only dates are approximate (first of month used). The stage stays proposed because the signed arrangement keeps statutory authority at ED and no operation of the referral process is documented; it could move to in_progress if referral or staff transfer is shown. The Civil Rights Division home page lists a joint ED and DOJ letter dated 2026-10-05 to state attorneys general on parents' rights; it was not opened and is not described as an OCR referral. Under the review rubric, an executive interagency arrangement toward a transfer that requires amending the Department of Education Organization Act is a parallel step, so even documented referrals would not by themselves lift the stage above proposed.
